newsitem.title: HAITI: U.S. to return paramilitary documents to Haiti.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to return paramilitary documents to Haiti.

text.p: Documents that U.S. troops seized two years ago from the headquarters of a brutal Haitian paramilitary group will be returned to the Haitian government within a week or two, U.S. officials said on Saturday.
"The documents are due to be shipped down this week, but that may slip due to transport issues," said Meg Gilroy, a spokeswoman for the U.S. embassy in Port-au-Prince.

The 160,000 pages of documents have been at the centre of a simmering dispute between the United States and Haiti's government, which had requested them to use in its investigation of human rights abuses during a three-year military dictatorship that ended in 1994 with the arrival of 20,000 U.S.-led troops.

The documents seized from the headquarters of the dreaded paramilitary organisation, the Front for Progress and Advancement for Haiti (FRAPH), are said to contain photographs of torture victims, membership applications, passports, identification cards and business records.
FRAPH has been blamed for much of the violence during the three years that followed a military coup. Human rights advocates said that violence claimed some 5,000 lives.

The United States had held the documents in spite of its own acknowledgment that they were Haitian property, saying it wanted to preserve the privacy of U.S. citizens whose names might be included in the pile of papers.
The documents will be returned with the names of U.S. citizens blocked out, embassy officials said. But they said negotiations were continuing over how the American names might be revealed.
"If the Haitian judicial sytem finds they need to know the name of a U.S. citizen to prosecute someone, then Washington would consider revealing the name," Gilroy said.
Human rights groups and the Haitian government have argued that the documents should be returned in their original condition.
Gilroy said half of the documents were already at the U.S. embassy in Haiti, and that the method of transporting the remainder was still being worked out.
